historical_record.description: Kezar Stadium and Pavilion went up at the park's southeast corner on Stanyan Street, on a site chosen after plans to complete the Golden Gate Park Stadium at the Polo Field were abandoned.
The Works Progress Administration replaced Kezar Stadium's wooden seating with concrete seating for 60,000 spectators.

The Recreation and Park Commission awarded the contract to rebuild and enlarge the press and broadcasting stand at Kezar Stadium, designed by the consulting engineer Thomas F. Chace, to Robert L. Wilson at $93,000, the lowest of five bids.

The Recreation and Park Commission unanimously named the press box at Kezar Stadium for its member William M. Coffman, after twenty years as a park commissioner, and ordered a bronze plaque placed in it.
The Recreation and Park Commission gave final approval to the Kezar master plan, whose transportation plan capped crowds at Kezar at 10,000 and set conditions for events of more than about 7,000.

The Recreation and Park Commission approved the schematic design for rebuilding Kezar Stadium after its demolition, due to begin in March: a football and soccer field with an all-weather track open to the community daily, a promenade around it, a landscaped buffer and about 10,000 seats.

The general manager reported the contract let for the reconstruction of Kezar Stadium, a job of more than $6 million long in planning; with bids slightly under the estimate, an improved track, night lighting, a sound system and an entry archway were all included, and work was to start at the end of March.

With its occupancy permit held up by fire inspection, the rebuilt Kezar Stadium's official opening was set for September 13, 1991, with a ribbon cutting by the mayor followed by the St. Ignatius-Washington High School football game.

The Board of Park Commissioners approved the plans for the club house at the new stadium in Golden Gate Park and awarded its general construction to the Coast Construction Company, the low bidder at $144,970.
The Board of Park Commissioners authorized Masten & Hurd, architects, to finish plans and specifications for enlarging Kezar Memorial Stadium.

With J. A. Bryant the low bidder on the enlargement of Kezar Memorial Stadium and not enough money yet for the whole job, the Board of Park Commissioners awarded him a first part of the work so the much-needed enlargement would not be delayed.

The Board of Park Commissioners appointed Masten & Hurd architects for the rehabilitation of Kezar Stadium under the Works Progress Administration, at six per cent of an estimated contract price of $35,000.
Because the Works Progress Administration was building the Kezar press stand to limits of time and money, features of the original plans were dropped and Masten & Hurd were paid $380 to revise them.
